newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli musicians try to drum up peace in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israeli musicians try to drum up peace in Hebron.

text.p: Israeli Eyal Davidov is trying to beat peace into Hebron with a set of African drums.
"(Music) brings peace more quickly than talks between the politicians," he said.
He started pounding out rhythms in the volatile West Bank city's central square on Monday, passing carved, hide-covered, wooden drums to Arab children and an Israeli soldier who came to play.
"All of the pictures from Hebron are very bad, you know people get killed. People get hurt. It's bloody," he said. "We want to show all the world it can be different."

Davidov, 27, is taking his musical trio from flashpoint to flashpoint trying to bring peace to Israelis and Palestinians. He has drummed with the ultra-Orthodox Jews of Mea Shearim and pounded out tunes with the Moslem children of Hebron.
"I hope that settlers will come and they can start to speak together and maybe there will be next year peace here," said Davidov, who learned his music during six years of travel in Africa.
But sometimes, he says, parents come to drag their children away.
"We're going to come here again and again," said fellow musician Lior Shay, 26. "We're going to show that it's possible to play music in a place that knows only violence."
About 50 Palestinian children gathered around Davidov and his trio, clapping, screaming and dancing.
They even cheered a gun-toting Israeli soldier who picked up a tune.

"If all the Israelis were like them (the trio), it would be a very good life," said Youssef Abu Sneineh, 15. "It doesn't matter if they're Israelis. What they're doing is not a problem. I am happy with this," he said.
At the same time, he said it would take more than music to bring peace.
"All this peace is a lie. Real peace is to get the Israelis out of the West Bank and Hebron."

About 400 Jewish religious settlers live in Hebron amid 100,000 Palestinians. The city has been a flashpoint of Israeli-Arab violence since July, when a right-wing Jewish woman pasted posters on storefronts depicting the prophet Mohammad as a pig.
The violence subsided when Palestinian police intervened four weeks ago, but still flares up occasionally.
"It's good that he (Davidov) comes and tries to communicate between the Arabs and the Jews," said one Israeli soldier, shaking his finger at kids who ventured too close to a Jewish settlement.
"But I don't know if he'll succeed."
About 30 yards behind him, four Jewish children stood, clapping to the beat, refusing to come any closer.
"Yuck," said one girl, about seven years old, wrinkling her nose. "I don't like the music."
"I don't want to tell you (why)," she said, as a younger girl piped in to explain why they would not play.
"I'm not friends with the Arabs," she said.
